etymology: From the Saxon blaest, a blowing or gust of wind; hence the scorching of standing corn by a hot, withering wind — in the Hebrew shiddaphon, the blight of the east wind that shrivels the ear before it fills.
biblical_def: Blasting is the scorching of the standing grain by a burning wind, so that the ear withers in the field before the sickle can be put to it. In Scripture it is never a bare accident of weather. It stands at the head of the covenant sanctions God swore against a disobedient Israel: “The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew” (Deu 28:22). The LORD claims the stroke as His own doing. Pharaoh saw it in his dream, where seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind” devoured the seven good ears (Gen 41:6), and Joseph read it as the word of God shewing to Pharaoh what He was about to do. Solomon, dedicating the temple, foresaw the day when blasting would drive Israel to her knees and asked that the prayer made toward that house be heard (1Ki 8:37). Amos names the purpose plainly: “I have smitten you with blasting and mildew … yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:9), and Haggai repeats it over a people who panelled their own houses while the LORD’s lay waste (Hag 2:17). Blasting, then, is a rod in a Father’s hand: a withered harvest sent to make a hard people ask why, and to send them home.
webster_summary: The scorching or blighting of grain by a hot wind; in Scripture a covenant judgment sent from the LORD’s own hand to summon a people to repentance.
webster_full: BLASTING, the act of blighting or withering; the destruction of corn or fruit by a scorching wind, mildew, or sudden heat.
From the Saxon blaest, a blast or gust of wind, and thence the injury such a wind inflicts upon growing grain.
Hebrew shiddaphon, from a root signifying to scorch; the east wind of Gen 41:6 that shrivelled the ears.
Ranked in Deu 28:22 among the covenant curses, and in 1Ki 8:37 among the calamities that send Israel to prayer.
Amo 4:9 and Hag 2:17 attribute blasting directly to the LORD as a chastening stroke.
scriptures: The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.
Gen 41:6
And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.
Amo 4:9

I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
Hag 2:17
I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The covenant sanctions upon the field are read either as ancient weather-superstition to be pitied, or their moral weight is transferred whole to a secular dread of the earth’s ruin — a substitute doctrine of last things with no Judge, no sin, and no Redeemer.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other across this word, and both empty it. The first says that Deu 28:22 is the guesswork of a pre-scientific people who blamed their gods for the weather; now that we understand fungus and wind, the theology may be quietly retired. But the passage does not offer a mechanism, it names an Agent: the LORD shall smite thee. Scripture nowhere denies second causes — there really was an east wind in Pharaoh’s Egypt — it denies that second causes are the last word. God governs the wind He made, and He governed it against a covenant people for a declared reason. The second error keeps the dread and discards the Judge. Where men no longer believe that a holy God visits sin upon a nation’s harvest, the fear of ruined fields does not disappear; it is transferred to a doctrine of last things without repentance, in which the earth is the offended party, guilt is measured by consumption rather than by God’s law, and the remedy is policy rather than a Mediator. That is not stewardship; it is the shape of religion poured into a mould that has no God in it. The Christian is bound to till and keep the ground faithfully (Gen 2:15) and to deal honestly with what he is given — and to refuse the counterfeit judgment day.

Recover what Scripture actually says about the ground. It is cursed for man’s sake (Gen 3:17), and the whole creation “groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now” (Rom 8:22), waiting not for a policy but for the manifestation of the sons of God. That groaning is real, and blight is one of its voices. Yet over the same ground stands an oath the flood could not break: “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease” (Gen 8:22). The believer therefore holds two things at once without panic: the field is under the curse and will sometimes wither, and the world will not slip out of the hands that hold it. Blasting is not the end of the world; it is a summons. Amos gives the refrain that interprets every failed harvest in redemptive history — yet have ye not returned unto me. The blighted ear is God’s question, and the only sufficient answer is repentance, faith in Christ, and the prayer Solomon asked God to hear when the corn failed.
roots_summary: A scorching wind upon the standing corn; in covenant terms, the LORD’s own stroke upon a nation’s bread to bring it back to Him.
roots_lines: Blasting — Saxon blaest, a gust or blast of wind; the blight such a wind works upon grain.
Hebrew shiddaphon, scorching; twinned in every occurrence with yeraqon, mildew.
Five appearances only: Deu 28:22; 1Ki 8:37; 2Ch 6:28; Amo 4:9; Hag 2:17 — all covenantal.
Gen 41:6 supplies the picture: ears “blasted with the east wind” in Pharaoh’s dream.
In Amos and Haggai the LORD speaks in the first person: I have smitten, I smote.
usage: Blasting is never bare weather in Scripture — the LORD says I smote you, and means it.
Deu 28 lists it among the sanctions; Solomon’s prayer treats it as a call to the house of God.
Amos’s refrain is the point of the rod: yet have ye not returned unto me.

etymology: From the Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew — the clammy blight that settles on the ear and turns it pale; the Hebrew yeraqon is named from its sickly green-yellow colour, the paleness of a wasting thing.
biblical_def: Mildew is the pale blight that settles upon standing grain and rots it where it stands, so that the ear looks fair and yields nothing. Hebrew names it by its colour, yeraqon, the yellow-green pallor of decay; and Scripture never separates it from its twin, blasting. The two go together in every place they appear, and every place is covenantal. They stand in the list of curses God swore against a disobedient Israel (Deu 28:22). They stand in Solomon’s dedicatory prayer, where the king asks that when blasting and mildew come, and a man knows the plague of his own heart and spreads forth his hands toward the house, God in heaven would hear and forgive (1Ki 8:37). They stand in Amos, where God claims them as His stroke and mourns the stubbornness that survived it: “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:9). And they stand in Haggai, upon a people who had leisure for their own ceiled houses and none for the LORD’s ruined temple: “I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me” (Hag 2:17). Mildew, then, teaches a hard mercy. God can leave a field standing and still take the bread out of it. He needs no army to humble a nation; a discolouring on the ear will do.
webster_summary: A pale blight upon growing grain; with blasting, one of the paired covenant judgments God sends upon the harvest to bring a people to repentance.
webster_full: MILDEW, a spot or blight upon plants and grain, arising from a clammy dew or damp; it turns the ear pale and spoils the increase.
From the Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew, the sweet clammy moisture on which the blight was thought to breed.
Hebrew yeraqon, from a root for green or yellow paleness — the colour of a wasting body or a blighted ear.
Named always with blasting: Deu 28:22; 1Ki 8:37; 2Ch 6:28; Amo 4:9; Hag 2:17.
The same Hebrew word is used of the paleness of men’s faces in terror (Jer 30:6).
scriptures: The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.

If there be in the land famine, if there be pestilence, blasting, mildew, locust, or if there be caterpiller; if their enemy besiege them in the land of their cities; whatsoever plague, whatsoever sickness there be;
Amo 4:9

I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
Hag 2:17
I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Chastening is read as bad luck. A blighted field is filed under misfortune, and the summons in it — the call to examine the heart and return — is never heard.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse of this word is not a redefinition of the fungus but a refusal of the doctrine. Scripture teaches that God governs the increase of the ground and withholds it deliberately; the modern instinct, even among churchgoers, is to sort every loss into accident and every gain into achievement, so that nothing that happens to a man is ever addressed to him. Solomon assumed the opposite. His prayer at the dedication takes it for granted that when mildew comes, the right response is a man knowing “the plague of his own heart” and spreading forth his hands toward the house of God. That is not superstition; it is covenant literacy. Nor does it license the cruelty of reading every man’s hardship as the wages of his particular sin — Job’s friends did that and were rebuked, and our Lord forbade it plainly of the Galileans and of the men of Siloam. The point is not that suffering decodes a private verdict; it is that suffering is not mute. It says: return. And the Lord who forbade the friends’ arithmetic gave the same word Himself — except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fatherly design of chastening. “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth” (Heb 12:6), and the rod on the field is of a piece with the rod on the soul. Mildew took nothing from Israel that God was not willing to restore the moment she turned; the whole tragedy of Amo 4 is the fivefold refrain of a God who kept knocking and a people who kept not answering. Read that chapter and count the strokes — cleanness of teeth, withheld rain, blasting and mildew, pestilence, overthrow — each followed by the same grieved sentence. Then read the end of it: “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.” The mercy in a blighted harvest is that it comes before that meeting and not after. It is a summons issued while there is still time to answer, and the believer who learns to hear the summons in small losses will not need the large ones.
roots_summary: The pale blight on the ear; with blasting, the covenant stroke that leaves the field standing and takes the bread out of it.
roots_lines: Mildew — Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew; the clammy blight on grain.
Hebrew yeraqon, paleness, the sickly green-yellow of decay.
Occurs five times, always paired with shiddaphon, blasting.
1Ki 8:37 and 2Ch 6:28 set it in Solomon’s prayer as an occasion for repentance and pardon.
Amo 4:9 and Hag 2:17 make God the express Agent: I have smitten, I smote.
usage: Mildew leaves the field standing and empties it — God can humble a nation without an army.
Solomon’s prayer treats mildew as the occasion for a man to know the plague of his own heart.
Chastening is never mute; it says return, and it comes before the meeting, not after.

etymology: From dear in its old English sense of costly or scarce, with the abstract ending -th; hence dearness of victuals, scarcity of bread — the state in which food is present but priced beyond the poor man’s reach.
biblical_def: Dearth is scarcity of food and the dearness of bread that follows it — famine considered from the side of the market and the empty purse. The Authorized Version uses it where corn is short and men must mortgage to eat. It falls upon the whole known world in Joseph’s day: “And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread” (Gen 41:54) — and that last clause is the whole doctrine of providence in eight words. God had sent a man before them, sold for a servant, to preserve life by a great deliverance; the dearth that emptied every other granary filled the one God had prepared. Stephen rehearses it before the council as the hinge of the patriarchal history (Act 7:11). Elisha meets a dearth in Gilgal and turns death in the pot into food for the sons of the prophets (2Ki 4:38). Nehemiah’s poor mortgage their lands and vineyards because of the dearth, and the reformer’s anger falls not on the weather but on the usurers who profited by it (Neh 5:3). And Agabus foretells a dearth throughout all the world, which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar (Act 11:28) — whereupon the church at Antioch immediately sent relief to the brethren in Judaea.
webster_summary: Scarcity of food and consequent dearness of provisions; in Scripture an appointed providence that both humbles nations and reveals whether mercy is in God’s people.
webster_full: DEARTH, scarcity; particularly a scarcity of provisions, and the high price which attends it; want of corn.
From dear, costly, scarce; the old English sense survives in speaking of a dearth of anything.
Distinguished in usage from famine chiefly by emphasis: famine names the want, dearth names the dearness.
Gen 41:54 and Act 7:11 apply it to the seven years foretold to Pharaoh and administered by Joseph.
Act 11:28 records the dearth foretold by Agabus in the reign of Claudius Caesar.
scriptures: And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
Act 7:11
Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance.

And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.
And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar.
corruption_summary: Scarcity is treated as a purely economic event with no Governor above it and no duty of mercy within it — a problem for policy rather than an occasion for providence and alms.
corruption_paragraphs: The common misuse of dearth is to hand it over entirely to management. Grain fails, prices rise, and the whole account is told in mechanisms — supply, harvest yields, hoarding, tariff — as though there were no throne above the field. Scripture tells the mechanisms too. It records Joseph’s twenty-per-cent levy in the years of plenty, his storehouses, his rationing, his land policy; the Bible is not squeamish about administration. But it insists the mechanism is the servant of a purpose: God sent a dreamer to Egypt in chains seventeen years before the first thin ear appeared, and the granary that fed the nations was built by a providence that Joseph’s brothers meant for evil and God meant unto good. Strip out that Governor and dearth becomes either blind misfortune or somebody’s fault, and the two answers between them exhaust the modern imagination. Scripture has a third: a Father who ordains scarcity and who has already, before the scarcity, prepared bread for those He means to keep.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that dearth tests the church’s bowels of mercy. Notice what happens the moment Agabus prophesies: the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, and sent it by Barnabas and Saul. No debate, no committee — a prophecy of hunger produced a collection. Nehemiah shows the negative pattern: when the dearth came, some in Judah used it to take their brethren’s fields in pledge, and Nehemiah confronted them until they restored what they had taken. Scarcity does not create character; it publishes it. The same want that turned some men into usurers turned others into the mercy of God with skin on. And behind both stands the Lord who fed Israel with manna, who multiplied loaves on a hillside, and who taught His people to pray daily for bread — that they might learn, in a year of dearth, whose hand had been feeding them all along in the years of plenty.
roots_summary: Scarcity of bread and dearness of price; the providence that emptied every granary but the one God had prepared beforehand.
roots_lines: Dearth — from dear, costly or scarce, with the abstract suffix -th.
Renders Hebrew ra‘ab (hunger, famine) and Greek limos in the New Testament.
Gen 41:54 — “the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.”
2Ki 4:38 sets a dearth at Gilgal, where Elisha heals the poisoned pottage.
Act 11:28 — Agabus foretells the dearth under Claudius; Antioch answers it with alms.
usage: Dearth names the dearness of bread, famine the want of it — the same providence seen from the purse.
God prepared the granary before He sent the scarcity; Joseph went down in chains seventeen years early.
A prophecy of dearth produced a collection at Antioch — scarcity publishes what a church is made of.

etymology: From the Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry; hence a want of rain, the parching of the ground — and in Scripture, by a bold figure, the parching of a man’s own soul under the hand of God.
biblical_def: Drought is the withholding of rain, and it is one of the plainest instruments of covenant discipline, because in Canaan there were no great rivers to fall back upon: Israel drank from heaven or not at all. Moses warned that disobedience would shut up the heaven that there be no rain (Deu 11:17); Elijah shut it by prayer for three years and a half in Ahab’s reign (1Ki 17:1); Haggai reports the LORD saying flatly, “I called for a drought upon the land” (Hag 1:11), and the drought lay upon the corn, the new wine, the oil, and upon the labour of men’s hands. Jacob knew drought as the herdsman’s ordinary hardship, consumed by heat in the day and frost by night (Gen 31:40). But the sharpest use of the word is inward. David, silent about his sin, describes the wasting of a conscience under conviction: “For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer” (Psa 32:4). An unconfessed sin dries a man out. And against that stands Jeremiah’s picture of the man whose trust is in the LORD: a tree planted by the waters, whose leaf is green, which “shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit” (Jer 17:8). Drought judges the shallow-rooted and proves the deep-rooted; the same dry season declares both.
webster_summary: Dryness; want of rain; and figuratively the parching of the soul under unconfessed sin — a season that exposes shallow roots and proves deep ones.
webster_full: DROUGHT, dryness; want of rain or of water; thirst; want of drink.
From the Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry.
Applied to the parched state of the ground and to the wasting of the body or spirit for want of moisture.
Hebrew choreb, parching heat, and tsimmaon, a thirsty ground (Deu 8:15).
Psa 32:4 uses it of the soul: “my moisture is turned into the drought of summer.”
scriptures: Psa 32:4
For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah.
Jer 17:8

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Hag 1:11

And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands.
Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.
corruption_summary: The inward drought is the one modern readers skip. Dryness of soul is diagnosed as a mood or a season to be waited out, when David traces it to a specific sin he would not name.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 32 is precise, and the precision is what gets lost. David does not say he passed through a dry stretch; he says God’s hand was heavy upon him day and night, that his bones waxed old through his roaring all the day long, and that his moisture was turned into the drought of summer — and he tells us exactly why: “When I kept silence.” The cause was concealed sin, and the cure was not the passage of time but confession: “I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” The counsel commonly given to a dried-out believer never gets near this. He is told his dryness is a phase, that everyone has them, that he should rest and be patient with himself. Sometimes that is true — there is a genuine dryness under affliction, and the saints have written of it honestly. But the first question David’s psalm puts is the one seldom asked: is there something you are keeping silence about? To skip that question is to leave a man roaring all the day long with the remedy in his hand and no one to tell him to open it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the dry season on purpose and provides against it beforehand. Jeremiah’s contrast is between the heath in the desert, which shall not see when good cometh, and the tree planted by the waters, which does not even notice the year of drought because its roots went for the river long before the rain stopped. Roots are grown in ordinary weather. The believer who reads, prays, sits under faithful preaching, and keeps short accounts with God in a green year is quietly sending roots toward the river; the one who lives on surface rain finds out what he was living on the first summer it fails. And when the drought is inward and does come, the LORD does not leave His people to it: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3). He who called for the drought is the same who ends it.
roots_summary: Want of rain upon the ground, and want of moisture in the soul; a season appointed to expose what a man’s roots have been reaching for.
roots_lines: Drought — Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry.
Hebrew choreb (parching heat) and tsimmaon (a thirsty land, Deu 8:15).
Deu 11:17 — disobedience shuts up the heaven that there be no rain.
Hag 1:11 — “I called for a drought upon the land”: the LORD names Himself the cause.
Psa 32:4 turns the word inward: conviction of unconfessed sin dries a man out.
usage: In Canaan there were no great rivers — Israel drank from heaven or not at all.
David’s drought of summer had a cause he names: when I kept silence.
Roots are grown in green years; the dry year only shows where they already went.

etymology: From the Latin vindemia, the grape-gathering, from vinum, wine, and demere, to take away; through the Old French vendange — hence the ingathering of grapes and the wine made of them.
biblical_def: The vintage is the grape harvest: the season when the clusters are cut, carried to the press, and trodden. It is the last ingathering of the agricultural year, and in a blessed year it runs so full that it overlaps the seasons on either side of it — “your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time: and ye shall eat your bread to the full, and dwell in your land safely” (Lev 26:5). That is covenant blessing in a single picture: no gap between harvests, no hungry month, plenty running into plenty. The curse reverses it. Isaiah tells the careless women that “the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come” (Isa 32:10), and Micah walks a stripped hillside like a man after the grapegleaners, finding no cluster to eat while his soul desires the firstripe fruit (Mic 7:1). Then the figure rises to its full height. Because the vintage ends in treading, and treading in red juice, the prophets make the winepress the emblem of the wrath of God, and set one Figure alone in it: “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” (Isa 63:3). John sees the same press in Revelation, and the sickle thrust into the vine of the earth. The vintage therefore ends in one of two cups: the wine of God’s house, or the wine of His fury.
webster_summary: The gathering of grapes and the wine so made; in Scripture the emblem both of covenant plenty and of the treading of God’s wrath.
webster_full: VINTAGE, the produce of the vine for the season; the gathering of the grapes and the making of wine.
From the Latin vindemia (vinum, wine, and demere, to take away), through the French vendange.
Hebrew batsir, the grape-gathering, from a root meaning to cut off or gather.
Lev 26:5 makes an overlapping vintage the sign of covenant blessing; Isa 32:10 makes its failure a judgment.
The treading of the vintage furnishes the prophets’ figure of divine wrath (Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19).
scriptures: Lev 26:5
And your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time: and ye shall eat your bread to the full, and dwell in your land safely.
Many days and years shall ye be troubled, ye careless women: for the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come.
Mic 7:1
Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.
Isa 63:3

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
corruption_summary: The winepress of wrath is edited out. Isaiah 63 and Revelation 14 are read as embarrassing survivals of a harsher religion, and the vintage is reduced to a harmless picture of abundance.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a persistent instinct to keep the vine and discard the press — to preach the clusters of Eshcol and the wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and to pass over in silence the day when the same fruit is trodden in fury. But the two belong to one image on purpose. Scripture chose the vintage for the figure of judgment precisely because the vintage was the year’s gladdest labour: singing in the vineyards, treaders shouting in the press, the juice running red over the stones. Isaiah takes that scene of joy and turns it inside out, and the horror of Isa 63 lies exactly in the contrast. To delete the press is not to make the Bible kinder; it is to leave the wine of God’s house resting on nothing, for the cup of blessing is only sweet because Another drank the cup of wrath. Strip out the fury and Gethsemane has no object: “let this cup pass from me” becomes an unaccountable dread over nothing at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the astonishing word alone. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me.” In Isa 63 the Treader is the Avenger, coming from Edom with dyed garments, and the blood on His raiment is His enemies’. Yet the church has never been able to read the verse without seeing the cross beside it, for there too He was alone: the disciples all forsook Him and fled, and no man stood with Him. The difference between the two treadings is which blood stains the garment. At Calvary He was trodden; at the last He treads. Between those two lies the whole of the gospel offer — that the Man who bore the press for sinners now holds it, and that every man alive will meet Him in one of the two vintages: gathered as fruit into the garner, or gathered as the vine of the earth and cast into the great winepress of the wrath of God (Rev 14:19).
roots_summary: The grape-gathering and its wine; in blessing an overlapping plenty, in judgment the treading of the wrath of God.
roots_lines: Vintage — Latin vindemia, grape-gathering, through Old French vendange.
Hebrew batsir, from a root to cut off; the last ingathering of the agricultural year.
Lev 26:5 — threshing reaching to vintage and vintage to sowing time is covenant plenty.
Jdg 8:2 and Isa 24:13 use the vintage and its gleanings for what little remains after a stripping.
Isa 63:3 and Rev 14:19 make the treading of the vintage the emblem of divine wrath.
usage: An overlapping vintage — no hungry month between harvests — is Leviticus’s picture of blessing.
The prophets chose the year’s gladdest labour for the figure of wrath, and the contrast is the point.
“I have trodden the winepress alone” — He was alone at the cross too, and the difference is whose blood.

etymology: From the Saxon staelc, akin to stele, a stem or handle; hence the standing stem of a plant which bears the ear — that without which the grain has nothing to grow on and nothing to grow from.
biblical_def: The stalk is the standing stem that carries the ear of corn. Scripture uses it in three places, and each is weighty. In Pharaoh’s second dream, “seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good” (Gen 41:5), and Pharaoh repeats it to Joseph — “seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good” (Gen 41:22). One stalk bearing seven full ears is superabundance; the seven thin ears blasted with the east wind that swallowed them are the famine that no plenty could withstand, and Joseph tells Pharaoh that the doubling of the dream means “the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.” In Joshua, Rahab hides the spies under the stalks of flax laid in order upon her roof (Jos 2:6) — a woman of Jericho covering the covenant people with the ordinary produce of her house, and finding mercy in the day the city fell. And in Hosea comes the sentence that governs the whole theme: “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal” (Hos 8:7). Israel’s religion had greenness without substance. Something came up; nothing came of it. A crop with no stalk cannot stand, and a bud with no meal cannot feed, and what the strangers do not swallow the whirlwind takes.
webster_summary: The stem of a plant which bears the ear; in Hosea the emblem of a religion that shows growth but yields no meal.
webster_full: STALK, the stem or main axis of a plant, which supports the leaves, flower, and fruit.
From the Saxon staelc; kindred with stele, a stem or handle.
Hebrew qaneh, a reed or stem (Gen 41:5), and qamah, standing corn (Hos 8:7).
Jos 2:6 uses the plural of flax stalks, laid in order upon a roof to dry.
Hos 8:7 — “it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal”: growth without substance.
scriptures: Gen 41:5
And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good.
And I saw in my dream, and, behold, seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good:
Hos 8:7
For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up.
Jos 2:6
But she had brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof.
corruption_summary: Hosea’s diagnosis is inverted. Visible growth is taken for proof of life, and a religion that shows leaf but yields no meal is counted a harvest because it looks green.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 8 describes a nation full of religious activity: kings set up, altars multiplied, calves cast, offerings brought. By any count of visible growth Israel was thriving. God’s verdict is that the crop has no stalk. The wind they sowed — their alliances, their innovations in worship, their borrowed gods — comes back as a whirlwind, and the bud that promised meal yields none. The error that stalks this word is the counting of buds. Where numbers, energy, and the appearance of growth are taken as the measure, a movement can be enormous and have no stalk in it: nothing that will stand when the wind rises, nothing that will feed a hungry soul. Our Lord walked the same field. Some seed sprang up quickly in stony ground, and the very speed of it was the symptom — because it had no deepness of earth, it withered when the sun was up. The remedy is not to despise growth but to ask Hosea’s question of it: is there a stalk? Will it stand? Is there meal in the bud?

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives the increase, and He gives it through means He has appointed rather than the means men invent. Pharaoh’s good stalk bore seven ears because God set them there; the doubled dream meant the thing was established by God. Hosea’s Israel had ears enough to look at and no stalk under them because they had sown the wind. Between those two stands the ordinary Christian labour of sowing what God actually commanded — the preached word, the ordinances, prayer, the plain duties of the household — and waiting on Him for the ear. “Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7) cuts both ways, and it cuts with particular sharpness against a church that would rather sow the wind and count the buds than sow the word and wait for the meal.
roots_summary: The stem that bears the ear; the difference between a crop that will stand and a greenness that yields nothing.
roots_lines: Stalk — Saxon staelc, akin to stele, a stem.
Gen 41:5, 22 — seven full ears on one stalk, the sign of Egypt’s seven plenteous years.
The doubling of Pharaoh’s dream meant, in Joseph’s words, that the thing was established by God.
Jos 2:6 — Rahab hides the spies under stalks of flax laid in order on her roof.
Hos 8:7 — sown wind, reaped whirlwind: no stalk, and the bud yields no meal.
usage: One stalk bearing seven full ears is plenty; seven thin ears swallowing them is famine God has established.
Hosea’s charge is growth without substance: something came up, nothing came of it.
Ask of any movement what Hosea asked of Israel — is there a stalk, and is there meal in the bud?

etymology: From bud, a shoot or unopened blossom, of uncertain Northern origin; hence to put forth buds. In Scripture the word carries the note of life appearing where none was expected — and, once, where none was possible.
biblical_def: To bud is to put forth the first shoot, the promise of fruit before the fruit. Scripture uses it of vines and pomegranates in their season (Gen 40:10; Son 6:11), but its great occurrence is a dead stick in a tabernacle. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram had risen against Moses and Aaron with the charge that all the congregation were holy, and wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the LORD? God answered first in judgment, and then, lest the question be reopened, He answered in a sign. Twelve rods, one for each tribe, Aaron’s among them, were laid up before the testimony, with the word: “the man’s rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom” (Num 17:5). “And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” (Num 17:8). Observe the piling of the stages: budded, buds, blossoms, almonds — a whole season in one night, on a cut branch that had no root and no soil. Eleven rods stayed dead. The priesthood is not seized, voted, or claimed by the sincerity of the claimant; it is given, and God vindicates His own appointment by making life come out of dead wood. That rod was kept in the ark for a token against the rebels (Heb 9:4).
webster_summary: Put forth buds; used above all of Aaron’s rod, which budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds in a night to vindicate God’s appointed priesthood.
webster_full: BUDDED, past tense of bud: to put forth or produce buds, shoots, or germs.
A bud is the gem or unopened shoot of a plant, containing the rudiments of leaf, flower, or branch.
Hebrew parach, to sprout or break forth into bloom (Num 17:8).
Used of the vine in Pharaoh’s butler’s dream (Gen 40:10) and of pomegranates in Son 6:11.
Num 17:8 records the budding of Aaron’s rod, laid up afterward in the ark (Heb 9:4).
scriptures: Num 17:8

And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.
Heb 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
And in the vine were three branches: and it was as though it budded, and her blossoms shot forth; and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes:
Son 6:11
I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded.
corruption_summary: Korah’s argument is perennial: since all the people are holy, no man may be set over them in the things of God. The budding rod is God’s standing answer, and it is the answer most resented.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah’s complaint sounds pious and is quotable to this day: all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them — wherefore then lift ye up yourselves? Every generation reproduces it. If the priesthood of all believers is true, why any ordained office at all? If the Spirit indwells every Christian, why should any man be set apart to preach, and why should the qualifications for that office be laid down as narrowly as they are in 1Ti 3 and Tit 1? The budding rod is God’s reply, and He gave it in a form no argument can touch. He did not debate Korah; He put twelve dead sticks in the dark and let one of them bloom. The priesthood is His to bestow. Under the new covenant every believer indeed has access through the one great High Priest, and the Levitical order is fulfilled and abolished in Him; yet the same God who ended the shadow appointed elders in every church, and He no more permits a man to seize that office than He permitted Korah to seize Aaron’s. “No man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Heb 5:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God vindicates His own appointments by giving life where there is none. The rod was cut wood. It had no root, no earth, no water, and one night; and in the morning it was carrying almonds, while eleven identical sticks lay beside it exactly as dead as they had been laid down. That is the pattern of everything God does through His ministers. The word preached is a dead stick until He makes it bud; the man who preaches it is dust and ash; and where fruit appears, no one can mistake whose hand did it. Aaron’s rod was then laid up in the ark beside the pot of manna and the tables of the covenant — bread from heaven, law from heaven, and life from dead wood, all three sealed under the mercy seat. It is not a stretch to see the whole gospel in that box, nor to see, in a rod that lived after it was cut off, the Branch out of a dry ground who rose on the third day.
roots_summary: To put forth the first shoot; supremely, a cut rod that budded, blossomed, and bore almonds in a night to seal God’s own choice.
roots_lines: Budded — past of bud, a shoot or unopened blossom; Hebrew parach, to break forth into bloom.
Num 17:5 — “the man’s rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom”: the test God Himself set.
Num 17:8 — four stages in one night: budded, buds, blossoms, almonds; eleven rods stayed dead.
The almond is the first tree of the Hebrew spring — the waking tree, the tree of hastening.
Heb 9:4 — the rod is laid up in the ark with the manna and the tables of the covenant.
usage: God did not argue with Korah; He put twelve dead sticks in the dark and made one bloom.
“No man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Heb 5:4).
Life out of cut wood is the pattern of all true ministry — no one can mistake whose hand did it.

etymology: From the Saxon clod, a lump or mass, kindred with clot and cloud; hence a lump of earth turned up by the plough — and, by an old and sober usage, the heavy soil of the grave.
biblical_def: Clods are the lumps of earth the plough turns up, which must be broken before seed can be sown. Isaiah makes them a parable of God’s teaching: “Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?” (Isa 28:24) — no, he ploughs for a season and then sows, each seed in its own place, the fitches beaten with a staff and the corn ground, but not for ever; “for his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him” (Isa 28:26). The husbandman’s measured wisdom is learned from God, and it is a picture of God’s own measured dealing with His people: He does not plough for ever, nor thresh beyond what is needed. Hosea sets Judah to plowing and Jacob to breaking his clods (Hos 10:11), and follows it with the summons to break up the fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, till He come and rain righteousness. Joel shows the reverse: “The seed is rotten under their clods” (Joe 1:17) — sown and lost, buried without a harvest. And Job, disputing the prosperity of the wicked, says that the clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him (Job 21:33): the grave receives him, and every man draws after him, as there are innumerable before him. The same soil that must be broken for seed will one day be broken for us.
webster_summary: Lumps of earth turned by the plough, which must be broken before sowing; also the soil of the grave — a figure both of God’s measured husbandry and of man’s end.
webster_full: CLOD, a hard lump of earth, of any kind; a mass of earth cohering; hence the ground, the earth, the turf.
From the Saxon clod, kindred with clot and cloud, all denoting a gathered mass.
Hebrew regeb, a clod of soil (Job 21:33; Joe 1:17), and telem, a furrow-ridge (Hos 10:11).
The husbandman breaks the clods after ploughing that the seed may find the earth (Isa 28:24).
Job 21:33 uses the clods of the valley for the covering of the grave.
scriptures: Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?
And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn; but I passed over upon her fair neck: I will make Ephraim to ride; Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods.
Joe 1:17
The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered.
The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him, and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him.
corruption_summary: Isaiah’s parable of the ploughman is read as farming advice rather than as what it is — a doctrine of God’s measured, purposeful, self-limiting dealing with His own people.
corruption_paragraphs: Isa 28:23–29 is one of the tenderest passages in the prophets, and it is commonly skimmed as an agricultural aside dropped into a chapter about drunkards and scoffers. It is nothing of the kind. Isaiah has been announcing a hard ploughing upon Judah, and he answers the fear that the ploughing will never stop. Does a farmer plough all day and never sow? Does he thresh bread corn for ever? He does not. He breaks the clods because he intends seed; he beats the fitches with a staff and not with a cart wheel, because the fitches are tender; he measures the instrument to the grain. And — this is the sentence that carries the doctrine — “his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him.” The discretion of the wisest farmer is a borrowed thing, learned from the God who is Himself the farmer of souls. Therefore the affliction upon a believer is measured, timed, instrument-matched, and aimed at a sowing. To read this as husbandry tips is to leave a suffering saint without the one comfort the passage was written to give.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the clods must be broken, and that God breaks them. Hosea sets the two halves side by side: Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves the easy work of treading out the corn — unmuzzled, eating as she goes — but God will put her to the plough. Then comes the call: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you” (Hos 10:12). Hard ground does not receive seed. A heart never broken has never been sown, whatever crop of religion is standing on the surface of it. And Job reminds us where the ploughing ends: the clods of the valley receive every man, and innumerable have gone before. The believer is not spared that soil; he is promised that the One who broke him for sowing will also, in the day appointed, break the ground open again.
roots_summary: Lumps of turned earth that must be broken for seed; the measured husbandry of God, and at the last the covering of the grave.
roots_lines: Clod — Saxon clod, a lump or mass; kindred with clot.
Hebrew regeb (Job 21:33; Joe 1:17); telem, a furrow-ridge (Hos 10:11).
Isa 28:24–26 — the ploughman does not plough for ever, and his discretion is taught him by God.
Hos 10:11–12 — Jacob shall break his clods; break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD.
Job 21:33 — the clods of the valley are the covering of the grave.
usage: The ploughman does not plough for ever — he breaks the clods because he intends seed.
“His God doth instruct him to discretion”: the farmer’s measured wisdom is a borrowed thing.
A heart never broken has never been sown, whatever religion is standing on the surface of it.

etymology: From the Saxon sicol, out of the Latin secula, from secare, to cut; hence the curved reaping hook drawn through standing corn — the plainest instrument of harvest, and therefore the Bible’s plainest instrument of judgment.
biblical_def: A sickle is the curved blade with which standing corn is reaped. In the law it marks the beginning of a sacred count: “begin to number the seven weeks from such time as thou beginnest to put the sickle to the corn” (Deu 16:9) — the seven weeks that run from the wave sheaf to Pentecost, and so from firstfruits to the great ingathering. The law also fences it with charity: a hungry traveller may pluck the ears with his hand in his neighbour’s field, but he shall not move a sickle unto his neighbour’s standing corn (Deu 23:25). Hunger may be fed; the harvest may not be stolen. Then the prophets take the tool up and put it into the hand of God. Joel hears the summons over the valley of decision: “Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great” (Joe 3:13). Our Lord uses it of the quiet certainty of the kingdom’s coming: when the fruit is brought forth, immediately He putteth in the sickle, because the harvest is come (Mar 4:29). And John sees it in the hand of a crowned Figure on a white cloud, one like unto the Son of man, with a sharp sickle; and “he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped” (Rev 14:16). The world ends as a harvest.
webster_summary: A curved reaping hook for cutting standing corn; in Scripture the instrument that begins the sacred harvest count and, at the last, reaps the earth.
webster_full: SICKLE, a reaping hook; an instrument with a curved blade for cutting grain.
From the Saxon sicol, Latin secula, from secare, to cut.
Hebrew chermesh (Deu 16:9; 23:25) and maggal (Joe 3:13; Jer 50:16).
Deu 23:25 permits plucking ears by hand in a neighbour’s field but forbids moving a sickle to it.
Greek drepanon, the reaping hook of Mar 4:29 and Rev 14:14–19.
scriptures: Deu 16:9
Seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee: begin to number the seven weeks from such time as thou beginnest to put the sickle to the corn.
When thou comest into the standing corn of thy neighbour, then thou mayest pluck the ears with thine hand; but thou shalt not move a sickle unto thy neighbour's standing corn.
Joe 3:13
Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
And he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped.
corruption_summary: The final harvest is emptied of its two outcomes. A reaping in which everything is gathered and nothing is burned is not the harvest Christ preached, and it is not good news.
corruption_paragraphs: The sickle is a dividing instrument. It cuts, and what it cuts goes two ways — into the garner, or into the fire. Christ’s own explanation of the tares leaves no room to soften it: the harvest is the end of the world, the reapers are the angels, and as the tares are gathered and burned in the fire, so shall it be. Where universal restoration is assumed — that all will be gathered in at last, that no one is finally lost — the sickle becomes a merely decorative image, and the urgency drains out of every gospel invitation. It cannot be had both ways. Either the Son of man on the white cloud reaps a field with two ends to it, or He does not, and Scripture is unambiguous that He does. Nor is this a hard doctrine bolted onto a kinder gospel; it is what makes the gospel news at all. Rev 14 sets the two reapings side by side: the harvest of the earth, and the vintage cast into the great winepress of the wrath of God. A man belongs to one or the other.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ripeness that governs the timing. Joel’s summons is not arbitrary: put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe — and the reason given is that their wickedness is great. God told Abraham that his seed would not return for four generations because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full; He waits, and His waiting is longsuffering, not indifference or inability. So too the Lord of the harvest in Mar 4:29 puts in the sickle when the fruit is brought forth, and not before. This should do two things to a believer at once. It should end all impatience with the delay of judgment — the Lord is not slack concerning His promise, but longsuffering, not willing that any should perish. And it should end all presumption upon that delay, for ripeness comes, and when it comes the reaping is immediate. The same sickle that begins the count at Deu 16:9 finishes it at Rev 14:16.
roots_summary: The curved reaping hook; it opens the sacred count from firstfruits to Pentecost and closes the age by reaping the earth.
roots_lines: Sickle — Saxon sicol, Latin secula, from secare, to cut.
Hebrew chermesh and maggal; Greek drepanon.
Deu 16:9 — the seven weeks to Pentecost are numbered from the first stroke of the sickle.
Deu 23:25 fences it with charity: pluck by hand, but move no sickle to thy neighbour’s corn.
Joe 3:13; Mar 4:29; Rev 14:14–16 put the sickle into the hand of the Lord of the harvest.
usage: Hunger may be fed by hand; the harvest may not be taken by sickle — charity and property together.
“Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” — the timing is governed by ripeness, not by impatience.
The sickle divides: into the garner or into the fire. A harvest with one outcome is not a harvest.

etymology: From plow (Saxon ploh, a ploughland) and man; the husbandman who drives the share through the ground. The Authorized Version spells it both plowman and plowmen, and the older English books freely ploughman.
biblical_def: The plowman is the man who breaks the ground for seed — the first labourer of the agricultural year and, in Scripture, a standing figure of patient, taught, hopeful work. Isaiah makes him a preacher: “Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?” (Isa 28:24). He ploughs a while and then sows, sets each seed in its appointed place, and threshes each grain with the instrument proper to it — “for his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him” (Isa 28:26). Every farmer’s good sense is a gift of common grace, and it images the discretion with which God deals with His own. When the heavens shut, the plowman is the first to be shamed: “Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads” (Jer 14:4). And when God turns the captivity of His people, the plowman is the measure of the blessing: “the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper” (Amo 9:13) — the harvest so long and so heavy that ploughing time comes round before the reaping is done. Isaiah promises that in the restored Zion strangers shall be their plowmen and vinedressers (Isa 61:5). Paul draws the ministerial lesson: “he that ploweth should plow in hope” (1Co 9:10).
webster_summary: One who ploughs the ground; in Scripture the emblem of labour taught of God, ashamed in drought, and overtaking the reaper in the day of blessing.
webster_full: PLOWMAN, one that plows or holds a plow; a husbandman; a cultivator of the ground; hence a rustic, a countryman.
From plow, Saxon ploh, a ploughland or measure of land, and man.
Hebrew charash, to cut or engrave, and so to plough; the participle is the plowman.
Isa 28:24–26 makes his measured method a parable of God’s instruction.
Amo 9:13 — “the plowman shall overtake the reaper”: a harvest that outruns the year.
scriptures: Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?
Jer 14:4
Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads.
Amo 9:13

Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt.
Isa 61:5
And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.
corruption_summary: Ordinary labour is treated as spiritually empty — a way to fund the real work rather than a calling in which God Himself instructs the workman to discretion.
corruption_paragraphs: A quiet error robs this word: the notion that manual, unremarkable, repetitive labour is at best neutral, a thing endured so that the important part of life can be paid for. Isaiah says otherwise about a man walking behind a plough in a field. The farmer’s knowledge of when to stop ploughing, what to sow where, which staff for the fitches and which cart wheel for the cummin — all of it, says the prophet, is because “his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him.” The competence of an honest workman is divine teaching. That is why Scripture can hand the plough back as a figure for the highest labour there is: he that ploweth should plow in hope (1Co 9:10), and no man having put his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God. The ploughman’s virtues — the straight furrow, the early start, the long patience between breaking ground and eating bread, the refusal to look behind — are the working Christian’s virtues, and they are learned in the field before they are named in the pulpit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is hope in the furrow. Jeremiah’s plowmen covered their heads because the ground was chapt and there was no rain; a man may break ground faithfully and see nothing come of it, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. But it sets against that the day the LORD promises through Amos, when the plowman shall overtake the reaper — the harvest so vast that the man coming to break ground for next year meets the man still gathering this year’s. That is what God intends for His labour in the earth. The minister who preaches into hard ground, the father who catechises children who do not seem to hear, the wife who prays for a husband year after year — all are plowmen, and all plow in hope, because the seed is not theirs, the rain is not theirs, and the day when the reaping outruns the ploughing has been promised by the mouth of the LORD.
roots_summary: The man who breaks the ground for seed; taught of God to discretion, ashamed in drought, and one day overtaking the reaper.
roots_lines: Plowman — plow (Saxon ploh, a ploughland) + man; Hebrew charash, to cut or plough.
Isa 28:24–26 — his measured method is a parable, and his discretion is taught him by God.
Jer 14:4 — in drought the plowmen are ashamed and cover their heads.
Amo 9:13 — the plowman overtakes the reaper when the LORD turns the captivity of His people.
1Co 9:10 — “he that ploweth should plow in hope”: the figure applied to gospel labour.
usage: The farmer’s plain competence is divine teaching: “his God doth instruct him to discretion.”
The plowman’s virtues — early start, straight furrow, long patience, no looking back — are the Christian’s.
Plowmen ashamed in the drought and plowmen overtaking the reaper are the same men in two seasons.
